articles.title: Court orders Russia to pay door factory US$3.6m for destroying business in Chernihiv Oblast
articles.body:
Chernihiv Oblast Commercial Court has ordered Russia to pay UAH 161.31 million (about US$3.54 million) in damages to Korfad LLC due to the destruction or significant damage of its production buildings in the city of Koriukivka.

Details: On 25 November 2025, during a large-scale Russian drone attack on Chernihiv Oblast, Russian drones struck an interior door manufacturing plant in Koriukivka.

According to an assessment by Expert Consulting Firm Desna-Expert LLC, the company sustained UAH 161.31 million (US$3.59 million) in damage after its buildings were struck directly by drones or hit by drone debris. Most of the buildings are now unusable. Specifically:

The court upheld the claims and ordered the full amount to be recovered from Russia, represented by the Russian Prosecutor General's Office, along with UAH 225,000 (US$5,000) in expenses for the technical inspection of the buildings and UAH 162,500 (US$3,600) for the independent damage assessment.

The founders of Korfad LLC (Koriukivka Door Factory) are Oleksandr Mysnyk, who also heads the company, Mykola Mysnyk, and Lidiia Mysnyk.

The Korfad website says the company produces panelled and flush interior doors and mouldings, using Italian Sincropan protective and decorative coatings. Its production facilities occupy an area of 15,000 sq m.

Background: Odesa Oblast Commercial Court has ordered Russia to pay UAH 291.59 million (US$6.49 million) in damages to Expansion Retail PrJSC after a missile strike destroyed the Fozzy shopping centre in Odesa.

articles.title: Rubio defends decision to invite Russia to G20 meetings
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has sought to defend Washington's invitation for Russia to participate in G20 meetings, emphasising the need to continue interaction with the Russian side.

Source: Rubio at a press conference in Atlanta following the G20 ministerial meeting, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Journalists asked Rubio to comment on criticism from his European counterparts regarding Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's participation in this week's G20 ministerial meeting and the invitation of Russian leader Vladimir Putin to the summit in Miami.

Rubio responded that he considers Russia's participation in G20 discussions important, particularly due to US diplomatic efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

Quote: "In order to end the war in Ukraine peacefully, you're going to have to have a negotiated settlement... How can you have a negotiated settlement between Russia and Ukraine if you don't have the ability to talk to both Russia and Ukraine? How can you talk to both Russia and Ukraine unless you interact with them?"

Details: Rubio said Lavrov's participation in the G20 ministerial meeting is another "opportunity to continue to interact with the Russian system".

Quote: "As I've said to you earlier in my conversations, the president does not view meeting with someone or talking to someone as legitimising everything they do or everything they stand for."

Details: According to Rubio, everyone wants to see a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, but it is impossible to make one without dialogue with Moscow.

Quote: "If we can play a role in mediating an end to that conflict, the United States is prepared to play that role. And to play that role, we have to have the ability to communicate with both sides. We talk to the Ukrainians plenty. We talk to them as much, if not more, than we talk to the Russian side."

Details: Rubio specifically stressed that Russia, like the US, is a nuclear power, and therefore Washington and Moscow must maintain dialogue to avoid dangerous escalation.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defence has downed 122 out of 168 Russian attack drones during day, 30 still airborne
articles.body:
Russian forces targeted Ukraine with 168 attack UAVs and an unspecified number of S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T drone- and air-launched cruise missiles during the day on Saturday. Ukraine's air defence has destroyed or jammed 122 UAVs and two S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T missiles.

Quote: "During the day on 31 October (from 06:30 to 19:30), the enemy attacked Ukraine with 168 attack UAVs (51 of them jet-powered), Gerberas and drones of other types, as well as S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T drone- and air-launched cruise missiles.

Early reports indicate that during this period, [Ukrainian] air defence forces destroyed or jammed 122 UAVs (37 of them jet-powered) and two S-8000 Banderol/Dan-T missiles."

Details: The Air Force noted that around 30 attack UAVs currently remain airborne.

articles.title: Debris from Russian drone falls at shopping centre in Kyiv, injuring child
articles.body:
A 12-year-old girl was injured when debris from a Russian drone fell at a shopping centre in Kyiv's Obolonskyi district.

Source: Kyiv City Military Administration

Quote: "In the Obolonskyi district, debris has fallen at a shopping centre. Early reports indicate that a woman has been injured."

Details: An air-raid warning was in effect in Kyiv from 17:53 to 18:37 due to the threat of Russian drones.

Update: Kyiv City Military Administration later clarified that the person injured in the Russian attack is a 12-year-old girl. She received medical treatment at the scene.

articles.title: Rubio says Zelenskyy may be invited to G20 summit
articles.body:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has suggested that Washington may invite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the G20 leaders' summit in December, particularly if his attendance could produce positive results.

Source: Rubio at a press conference in Atlanta, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Rubio was asked whether the Ukrainian president will be invited to the G20 summit in Miami on 14-15 December, to which Russian leader Vladimir Putin has also been invited.

He answered that the decision is up to US President Donald Trump.

Quote: "Look, that's a leaders-level meeting. That would be up to the president to decide. I wouldn't rule it out, especially if something positive could happen as a result of him [Zelenskyy – ed.] attending. But I don't have an announcement on that today."

articles.title: Türkiye's Erdoğan calls on Russia and Ukraine to act responsibly in Black Sea
articles.body:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has condemned attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea, urging both sides, Russia and Ukraine, to act responsibly regarding this issue.

Source: Erdoğan at a joint press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Istanbul, as reported by European Pravda

Details: The Turkish president pointed to the escalation in the Black Sea, stating that attacks on civilian vessels would not benefit either side.

Erdoğan stressed that the attacks are absolutely unacceptable to Türkiye, regardless of who carries them out or how they are justified. He urged all parties to act responsibly in this matter.

Erdoğan said Türkiye is continuing talks with the parties involved on restoring maritime security in the Black Sea. He believes an agreement on this issue could help advance diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine and achieve lasting peace.

He added that Türkiye plans to discuss the matter with Russia.

The Turkish president also said Türkiye has reaffirmed its support for the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine, which it considers a strategic partner.

articles.title: Drone violates Moldovan airspace amid Russian attacks on Ukraine
articles.body:
A drone violated Moldova's airspace during Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine on Saturday 31 October.

Source: European Pravda, citing Moldova's Ministry of Defence

Details: Amid massive Russian attacks on Ukraine, the Moldovan National Army's Air Operations Centre reported an unauthorised drone flight in Moldovan airspace.

The drone was detected at 16:24, flying from the village of Semenivka in Ukraine's Odesa Oblast towards the village of Plopi in the Rîbnița district in the unrecognised breakaway region of Transnistria.

The drone was later spotted near the settlement of Bănești, Telenești district.

For security reasons, the military introduced airspace restrictions over northern and central Moldova.

At 16:54, the drone disappeared from the Defence Ministry's radar near the village of Țibirica in Călărași district.

Moldova's Defence Ministry said it continues to monitor the country's airspace. It urged people not to approach any suspicious aircraft or debris they might find and to call the emergency services on 112 immediately.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine and Türkiye have agreed to work on Black Sea grain corridor
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he and his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdoğan have agreed to work to restore the grain corridor and ensure maritime security in the Black Sea.

Source: Zelenskyy at a press conference in Istanbul, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Zelenskyy stressed that Russia has been worsening the security situation in the Black Sea with its aggression since 2014. The president noted that Türkiye supports Ukraine's efforts to restore maritime security in the region.

Quote: "Türkiye consistently supports our sovereignty, our territorial integrity, and our steps that can protect safe shipping in the Black Sea and bring normal life back to the region."

Details: Zelenskyy added that he and Erdoğan had discussed "some ideas and proposals that can help".

Quote: "The president [Erdoğan] and I have agreed to work on the Black Sea grain corridor so that the corridor exists and is effective."

articles.title: Zelenskyy and Erdoğan discuss involving Türkiye in negotiations to end war
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan have discussed Türkiye's possible involvement in peace talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine and the prospect of the talks being held in Türkiye.

Source: Zelenskyy in a comment to the press alongside Erdoğan in Istanbul

Quote: "We're currently preparing for a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, the US and Russia in the first half of November. Mr President and I have discussed the prospects for the meeting and other options, including the possible involvement of Türkiye, Europe and all our partners, as well as the possibility of a meeting here in Türkiye."

Details: Zelenskyy stressed that "strong decisions are needed to achieve peace, and signals must be sent to Russia at all levels that there is no alternative to peace and that support for Ukraine will continue".

articles.title: Three injured in Russian attack on Ukrainian coal facilities
articles.body:
Three employees were injured when Russian forces launched a massive attack on coal-mining facilities belonging to DTEK Energo in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.

Source: press service for DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company

Details: The attack caused severe damage to industrial buildings at the facilities.

All three employees injured in the attack have received medical treatment. DTEK said their condition is stable.

Background: On the night of 30-31 October, Russia attacked energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast yet again.

articles.title: Finnish president says he conveyed two messages from Zelenskyy to Putin
articles.body:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said he conveyed two messages from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Vladimir Putin during a phone call with the Russian leader on 27 October.

Source: Stubb in a programme on the Finnish broadcaster Yle, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Stubb said he had relayed two messages from Zelenskyy to Putin. The first concerned Zelenskyy's willingness to hold direct talks with Putin, particularly on territorial and security issues. The second outlined Kyiv's proposals for de-escalation: possible ceasefires covering energy facilities, food security, prisoner-of-war exchanges and infrastructure more broadly.

The Finnish president added that he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre had also been able to ask Putin about Russia's preparations for the trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. He said the call had been useful because it gave them a chance to find out how Putin planned to approach the talks.

Asked whether the call with Putin had brought peace closer, the Finnish president said it was more of a confidence-building step. Stubb added that they had made no backward steps, but the first call was primarily about establishing trust.

The president was also asked what would come next in terms of restoring contact and relations with Russia after the phone call. Stubb said there is no need to rush and that things should be taken step by step. He added that relations between Finland and Russia, for example, would be completely different from what they had been in the past.

Stubb said Finland and Norway had also told Putin that they oppose the Russian shadow fleet's activities in the Baltic Sea.

Finnish president says Putin gave no history lectures during phone call
articles.body:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has denied media reports that Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin lectured him and the Norwegian prime minister on history during a phone call.

Source: Stubb in a programme on the Finnish broadcaster Yle, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Asked by a journalist to comment on a Financial Times report that Putin spent most of the phone call telling the Finnish and Norwegian leaders about the "initial reasons for the conflict" with Ukraine, Stubb denied this, saying the reports were false.

Stubb said Putin had given his version of what happened after 2014 – the annexation of Crimea and the war in Ukraine's east.

Putin also talked about the peace talks held in Istanbul after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Finnish leader noted.

The president stressed that he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre had called Putin at Ukraine's request. He added that Finland and Norway also have their own security interests and, as Russia's neighbours, would have to establish contact with Moscow sooner or later.

Finland is not acting as a mediator in the negotiations but fully supports Ukraine, Stubb stressed. He said Finland stands 100% with Ukraine and that Putin had been told this directly.

Stubb acknowledged that the phone call with Putin had drawn criticism from some leaders but said he is not concerned about a rift between the Nordic countries.

The Finnish president stressed that all the Nordic countries share exactly the same goal in this matter, namely supporting Ukraine and facilitating the peace talks, so he is not worried in this regard.

articles.title: Turkish president receives Zelenskyy in Istanbul
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdoğan after arriving in Istanbul on Saturday 31 October.

Source: the Turkish president's press service, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Erdoğan welcomed the Ukrainian president to his Dolmabahçe residence in Istanbul.

After an exchange of greetings between the delegations, Erdogan and Zelenskyy proceeded to hold one-on-one talks.

The talks between the delegations are attended by Turkish Defence Minister Yaşar Güler, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, İbrahim Kalın, Head of Türkiye's National Intelligence Organisation, and Rustem Umierov, Head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service.

The Ukrainian president reported that the talks with the Turkish leader would focus on bilateral partnership and diplomatic prospects for ending the Russia-Ukraine war. The presidents will also discuss maritime security in the Black Sea.

articles.title: Ukraine's human rights chief provides details about people evacuated from Oleshky: oldest is 94 – photos
articles.body:
The oldest person evacuated from occupied Oleshky is 94 years old, and the youngest is just over a year old; their pets were also evacuated alongside them.

Source: Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian Parliamentary Human Rights Commissioner, on X (Twitter)

Quote: "The oldest evacuee is 94 years old, while the youngest is just over one year old! Another woman will celebrate her 49th birthday tomorrow!"

Details: Lubinets described how one of the evacuated families had been fighting for survival in their home in Oleshky after it was severely damaged in a Russian attack.

Quote: "Due to his health condition, the father was unable to make his way down from the eighth floor on his own, as the staircases had been destroyed. It is frightening even to imagine the conditions in which these people were living: they were effectively cut off from access to food and water. But that is now behind them – the family is safe."

Details: Another evacuated man from Oleshky survived 16 Russian drone attacks and four missile strikes on his own home. One of the explosions occurred just one metre from the wall of his house.

Quote: "Along with the residents, we also managed to evacuate their beloved pets: dogs, cats, a parrot, and even a raccoon!"

Background: On 31 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that a humanitarian operation in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, has been successfully completed. All evacuated Ukrainian citizens have crossed the border into Ukraine in Chernihiv Oblast.

articles.title: UK tells Putin via his foreign minister that he will not win war
articles.body:
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has confronted his Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov at a meeting of G20 foreign ministers in the US.

Source: Sky News, as cited by European Pravda

Details: At the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, Miliband addressed Lavrov directly, calling Russia the aggressor and reminding him of the war crimes committed by Russian forces against Ukrainians.

Quote: "Let me say this directly to the Russian foreign minister – we all know who the aggressor in this war is. Let's talk about what happened at Dnipro railway yesterday. Only yesterday your drones attacked and killed 15 people. And there are countless examples like this of you killing innocent civilians throughout this war. We all know you are the aggressor."

Details: In his address to Lavrov, Miliband stressed that Russia is not winning this war thanks to the courage of the Ukrainian people and the help of allies.

Quote: "Putin thought then he would win this war easily. But you are not winning this war. Thanks to the courage of the Ukrainian people and the solidarity of countries round this table, you are not winning. If you had the courage to tell the truth and to do what is right you would tell Putin that he is not winning this war and will not win."

articles.title: Russia's Lavrov showed no willingness to make peace at G20 meeting, EU's chief diplomat says
articles.body:
Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, has said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov's stance at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in the US gave no indication that Russia is willing to engage in peace talks.

Source: AFP, as cited by European Pravda

Details: Asked by a journalist whether Lavrov had indicated at the meeting that Russia is willing to make concessions to end the war, Kallas said he had not.

She noted that even if Russian officials were to claim otherwise, their actions would tell a different story. She stressed that Russia must demonstrate through its actions that it is willing to negotiate.

Quote: "July, August and September were the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine."

Details: The EU's top diplomat noted that Lavrov had voiced false information about the war in Ukraine at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting.

Quote: "Of course, he put forward a lot of lies and many false claims, which we were also able to refute afterwards."

Details: Kallas called for continued pressure on Russia, notably to secure a ceasefire in the Black Sea.

Asked why the traditional group photo had not been taken at the foreign ministers' meeting, Kallas replied: "We must not normalise war crimes around this table."

articles.title: Ukrainian soldiers use drone-mounted net launcher to trap Russian soldier – video
articles.body:
The Ukrainian military has used a drone-mounted net launcher to help kill a Russian infantryman on the front line.

Source: Ptashka Drones, a company that develops and manufactures net launchers

Details: Ptashka Drones said soldiers from the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade used a drone-mounted net launcher against the Russian soldier. They initially attempted to strike him with an FPV drone but missed. Another drone then dropped a net on the soldier, trapping him.

The company said the Russian soldier was unable to free himself from the net and was later killed by soldiers from the 3rd Assault Brigade using FPV drones.

The Ptashka net launcher is a reusable weapon against FPV drones. It comes with several net cartridges, each costing between US$27 and US$33. The company has developed interception systems for both FPV drones and reconnaissance UAVs such as the Mavic, Autel and Matrix.

The nets designed to intercept FPV drones measure 3.7 × 3.7 m, and the recommended firing distance is 1-10 m.

Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that Ukrainian forces had downed a Russian Molniya attack drone using an interceptor drone equipped with a Ptashka net launcher.

articles.title: Ceasefire in Kherson Oblast: Russia attempting to discredit Ukrainian defence forces
articles.body:
The Russians are attempting to discredit the Ukrainian defence forces during a humanitarian mission in temporarily occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast.

Source: Maksym Kravchuk, spokesperson for the Pivden (South) Group of Forces, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda

Quote: "The Ukrainian defence forces, specifically units from the Pivden Group of Forces, are abiding by the agreements within the framework of the ceasefire in the area of the humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky.

Meanwhile, the enemy has been using the pause for military purposes: the Russian military has rotated units, fortified positions, installed anti-drone protection on roads, strengthened logistics, and brought in ammunition. The enemy's claims to the contrary are false. The Ukrainian military is strictly observing the ceasefire, and Russian provocations have been recorded."

Details: Kravchuk stressed that Ukrainian units have repeatedly spotted Russian reconnaissance drones during the ceasefire and documented Russian troops dropping munitions from drones in an effort to discredit Ukrainian forces and portray them as violating the agreement.

The Pivden Group of Forces stressed that the ceasefire is strictly humanitarian in nature and is intended to provide assistance to civilians and evacuate them to Ukrainian-controlled territory.

Units from the Pivden Group of Forces are monitoring the situation and tracking Russian actions to prevent possible threats and provocations, Kravchuk noted.

Food Lines, War Dead: The Way They Live Now In A Frigid Siberian Town
articles.body:
For a few days in mid-October, residents of Tura, a remote town in Siberia's vast taiga, might have been excused if they thought they were back in the U.S.S.R. One woman, in fact, said the situation was "worse than it was under the Soviets."

With temperatures hitting minus 15 Celsius, locals young and old stood in line for hours at a time outside the main food shop to buy a few bare necessities such as potatoes, cabbage, eggs, and milk and to fathom the precipitous prices they had to pay if they managed to reach the counter.

Efforts to establish a system allowing customers to head back to the relative warmth of their homes and return when their number came up --- a common tactic amid the frequent food shortages of the Soviet era -- fell flat.

"The vendors said, 'If you want to eat, you have to wait in line,'" said Svetlana, whose last name is being withheld for her safety. "There were no exceptions, even for children or the elderly."

"Then they started limiting quantities, no more than 1 kilogram per person. Literally something like a single potato for each family member, and every family member has to show up to get it," Svetlana said. "It's come to this: great Russia, rationing potatoes."

The shortages did not stem from Russia's invasion of Ukraine, although the nearly five-year full-scale war has taken a heavy toll on the town, claiming at least 34 men among its 4,000 residents and damaging its economy.

Instead, they resulted from a combination of formidable logistical challenges and poor planning -- a problem that is pervasive and sometimes deadly in Russia.

No road reaches Tura from Krasnoyarsk, the regional capital over 1,000 km to the southwest, and the town's lifeline is the Nizhnyaya Tuguska River. When low water levels made it unnavigable in July, authorities failed to establish an adequate alternative supply route, and shortages of many fresh foods hit this month.

Prosecutors have launched a criminal investigation against several officials on suspicion of negligence.

Some items such as fruit, meat, dairy products, flour, and bottled water all but disappeared, and prices more than tripled by official counts.

"Look at these prices: 1,100 to 1,300 rubles ($13-16) for a kilo of cucumbers," Svetlana said, adding that cucumbers had run out before her turn came. "1,800 ($22) for green onions, 1,000 for onions! Forget about peppers and tomatoes."

Olga, another local resident, said her mother had to come to the store because the staff wouldn't let her buy the elderly woman's share on her behalf.

Other families "brought little children with them. Otherwise, they wouldn't have given out rations for each person -- even though the saleswoman knows how many people are in the family," Olga said. "We didn't have such horrors even under the Soviets, my mother said. She remembers."

After a major crunch in mid-October, food is now being flown in by air and rationed, with limits on how much a single person or a family can buy.

But the most recent shipment was missing potatoes, onions, and cabbage after two flights were postponed due to weather. Food lines have persisted despite the resumption of air deliveries.

On October 21, the district administration reported that food supplies at several local schools would not last past the end of the month. Residents say the food that has been flown in has been bought up quickly, and they worry about getting through the winter. When the river freezes over, though, it can serve as a road.

"The shop assistants are trying to reassure us, saying there's still some grain left over, pasta, canned goods," Svetlana said. "What, are we going to feed the kids canned goods all winter?"

For some, the town's current predicament is a result of developments that have altered life in Tura over the years, both before and after Russia launched its war against Ukraine.

"Back then, we fed ourselves [by] hunting and fishing. And the supplies [brought in by the state] were plentiful," Olga said of the Soviet era. "Now there are no fish in the river, no reindeer."

Tura is at the heart of an area once populated mainly by Evenks, members of an ethnic group of traditionally nomadic reindeer herders who have lived in Siberia and other parts of North Asia for centuries. About 900 of Tura's 4,000 residents have Evenk roots.

The town was built on the site of an Evenk camp in 1927 and was the seat of the Evenk Autonomous District until President Vladimir Putin's government folded it into the Krasnoyarsk Krai in 2007, a downgrade at the hands of a state that activists say is suppressing the cultures of indigenous groups and other minorities.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the state has lured men to the front by offering substantial benefits and signing bonuses, incentives that are particularly attractive in economically struggling regions where jobs are scarce.

Among numerous reports with similar findings, a March 2025 report from the US-based Wilson Center think tank said men from Russia's indigenous communities "have been recruited at above-average rates and experienced higher-than-average combat death rates."

"About 20-25 of us [Evenks] have gone [to war] over the past four years," Tura resident Kachikan said. "Half have already died. Six have been buried, but there are some who have been missing for a long time, so it's unlikely they'll be found alive."

"Two members of the Udygir family have already [been killed], Timur and Romka. They're cousins, Oleg and Yury's sons. Dmitry, who's also related, hasn't been in touch in a while; there'll be a death notice about him soon, too," Kachikan said.

"He went on a contract. It's obvious why: to make money," he said. "There's no work here. The oil industry? They don't hire our people, only shift workers. You can't even get a job as a cook."

Another Evenk, Volodya Oyogir, "went missing in 2025, and there was a funeral this year; he was declared dead. His wife had been searching for him since the previous March," Kachikan said.

"Volodya was a good hunter from a prominent family," he said, pointing to his grandfather Nikolai Oyogir, a prominent Evenk poet and folklorist who died in 1988. "His poems were published in Soviet journals, he worked at a newspaper. And his grandson died in the war. Such is fate."

A database maintained by the Russian-language outlet Mediazona lists 34 war dead from Tura. It includes the Udygir cousins, who died at age 30 and 42, respectively, and Oyogir, who was 37 when he was declared dead.

"What kind of life is this? Folk crafts have been destroyed. Fishing has effectively ceased as a source of income," said Vladimir, a Tura resident.

"The Tunguska has been flooded with oil, so there are almost no fish left," Vladimir said, apparently referring to spills that polluted the river in 2023 and 2024.

"The nearest reindeer herds are beyond Surinda," a settlement some 400 kilometers away, he said. "There's no real government support, and the prices are exorbitant. That's why people go to this [war]."

Siberia.Realities is a regional news outlet of RFE/RL's Russian Service.

articles.title: Evacuation From Russian-Occupied Oleshky Completed, Kyiv And Moscow Say
articles.body:
Evacuation of residents from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky had been completed as Moscow and Kyiv continued to stick to the temporary cease-fire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.

Buses filled with civilians left the war-torn area for the first time in more than four years without incident, both parties have reported, with the localized cease-fire set to remain in effect until November 1.

No media source currently available

Russian ⁠human rights ombudswoman Yana Lantratova said in a social media post on October 30 that after arriving in Ukraine's Russia-occupied Crimea, one convoy of buses then headed toward Russia, while a second convoy was bound for Ukraine.

"We are concluding our humanitarian mission ⁠in Oleshky. ‌We are currently in the territory of Armyansk (in northern Crimea)," she said in a video posted on Telegram, adding that both sides had praised the high standard of its organization.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said those residents of Oleshky who wished to travel to Ukraine have crossed into the country on October 31, thanking the United States and Melania Trump for their mediation.

After reaching Anapa in southern Russia from Crimea, the civilians were flown to the Belarusian city of Homel and then transported by bus to Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region.

The circuitous route was needed to avoid roads along front lines that have been heavily mined and destroyed by the conflict, sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"When the world pays attention, people are rescued. Further steps toward de-escalation and real progress toward peace are also needed," Zelenskyy wrote.

Before the evacuation, Oleshky residents had been trapped for months in the largely ruined city, which was cut off from the outside world, with little to no access to food, drinking water, medicine, or electricity.

"Until we got on the buses, we were still afraid," Oleshky evacuee Liubov told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service on October 31. "We were so worried and nervous. Before that, we couldn't sleep at night, wondering how this would go."

As the evacuation from the war-torn city was unfolding on October 30, the Kremlin said the temporary cease-fire there should not be extrapolated to the broader peace settlement process in Ukraine.

Moscow has repeatedly said it was not seeking a partial easing of the conflict, urging a complete resolution that would include its demands, including full control over Ukrainian territories that Russian forces have been unable to seize on the battlefield.

Separately, Russia has intensified its airstrike campaign aimed at pressuring Kyiv into accepting its conditions for peace by attacking the country's energy and civilian infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid cold weather.

This year, however, the Ukrainian military has been increasingly responding to the attacks with campaigns of its own, targeting energy and military infrastructure inside Russia with long-range drone strikes.

On October 31, the Ukrainian military claimed that it had targeted the Russian state-owned Kombinat Kamensky chemical and defense enterprise in the Rostov region, using both drones and Neptune coastal missile systems.

It said that a “fire at a finished-products warehouse has been confirmed,” with damage reported to four production workshops, adding that the facility manufactures solid rocket propellant for ammunition used by multiple Russian missile systems.

The Rostov region, which borders Ukraine, is a strategically important industrial and logistics hub in southwestern Russia. Earlier in the month, Reuters reported that Russia had nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones there in just six weeks.

Citing satellite imagery, the report said the site had been an empty field as of the end of August and had become a complex facility covering an area equivalent to around 126 soccer fields by mid-October.

Rostov has been under Ukrainian aerial attacks since September. The Ukrainian Security Service had earlier claimed to have targeted a number of “Russian aerial assets” in a special operation at a military airfield in the regional capital, Rostov-on-Don.

The US State Department has announced the approval of a critically needed sale of Patriot air defense interceptors to Ukraine worth $2.1 billion to strengthen Kyiv’s defenses against increasing Russian aerial attacks.

Zelenskyy, however, warned that the 500 missile interceptors could take “several years” to arrive.

Welcoming the US State Department’s move as a “strong decision,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post that “500 PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number” and could form an effective defense package this winter, but noted that “deliveries may begin only in a few years.”

“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said while noting that that his country’s energy infrastructure is under Russian attacks.

The State Department said that the proposed sale of the missile interceptors, being purchased with funds from Canada, Germany, and Norway, will support the foreign policy and national-security objectives of the United States “by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe.”

The announcement of the proposed sale came after Zelenskyy repeated his calls on October 30, asking the United States to speed up the release of the interceptors, which are seen as the most effective weapon against the ballistic missile attacks from Russia.

In September, the European Commission approved 6.1 billion euros ($6.82 billion) in defense procurement for Ukraine.

This amount also included the purchase of US PAC-3 Patriot missile interceptors under special exception to EU rules. The European Commission did not specify how much money was allocated for these interceptors, citing operational security considerations.

At a closed-door meeting of the European Council in October, Zelenskyy told the participants how many Patriot interceptor missiles Ukraine would need to get through the winter.

Daud Khattak is a senior international correspondent covering the Near East in RFE/RL’s Central Newsroom. He was previously the managing editor of RFE/RL's Radio Mashaal.

RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service has seen its audience grow significantly since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 and is among the most cited media outlets in the country. Its bold, in-depth reporting from the front lines has won many accolades and awards. Its comprehensive coverage also includes award-winning reporting by the Donbas.Realities and Crimea.Realities projects and the Schemes investigative unit.

Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
articles.body:
After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.

Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practising "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."

Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.

Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.

Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition, and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia, an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focussed on making changes in domestic politics, and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: More than 290 arrested in France as some weekend protests turn violent
articles.body:
Protests continue across France as 320,000 people take to the streets over rising living costs and poor school conditions for a third consecutive weekend, with clashes reported in several cities.

A number of clashes have been reported between protesters and police in several French cities on Saturday as hundreds of thousands of people again took to the streets nationwide to protest the rising cost of living and conditions in schools.

The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people had participated in demonstrations across the country, including 70,000 in Paris.

"The marches proceeded smoothly within the framework of the declared demonstrations," the ministry said, while noting that "radical elements" in several cities, including Bordeaux, Toulouse and Marseille, had attempted to enter city centres "with the aim of carrying out vandalism and looting."

In Marseille, footage showed fires burning in the streets as firefighters responded. Clashes with police were also reported in Rennes and Toulouse.

After a largely peaceful start to the day, police fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon in the late afternoon, according to French media reports and live broadcast footage. Tensions in the capital escalated as demonstrators reached the end of their march on the city's southern outskirts.

Footage aired by BFMTV showed fireworks exploding and incendiary devices being thrown at officers in riot gear, with several officers caught in the flames.

Paris police carried out more than 1,200 checks at railway stations and nearby areas early on Saturday to identify potential troublemakers, the city's police prefecture said.

The checks aimed to prevent demonstrators from bringing fireworks, knives and other prohibited items to the marches.

Police also deployed "all available resources" in the air to monitor security throughout the day, the prefecture said. An official order authorized camera-equipped drones to capture and transmit live images of the situation across the capital.

More than 290 arrests were made on Saturday across France, according to police.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned earlier Saturday that the demonstrations posed a "very high risk," citing calls for looting and rioting.

Around 70,000 police officers and other security personnel were deployedacross the country to maintain order during the protests.

Authorities also feared that Halloween celebrations could give people an opportunity to conceal their identities while committing offenses.

Amid concerns over attacks on public buildings and looting, officials ordered protest routes in Paris and other cities to be moved away from city centers.

Many shops and businesses responded by boarding up their windows and taking other precautions. Curfews and other restrictions were also imposed in several cities, including measures targeting specific areas and minors.

A similarly large security deployment last weekend largely prevented a repeat of the violence and destruction seen during the October 17 protests.

Young people have been taking to the streets for weeks to protest inadequate staffing and equipment in schools. Since mid-October, other groups have joined the demonstrations, mainly over the rising cost of living.

Trade unions, school and student organizations, and the grassroots Yellow Vest movement, which first rose to prominence in France in 2018, called for Saturday's protests.

articles.title: Gen Z protests sweep cities across Germany
articles.body:
Young people in Germany have taken to the streets in some 34 cities, calling for greater political say and a more hopeful future. The protests come amid a wave of youth demonstrations across Europe. DW has more.

This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31, 2026:

The German protests on Saturday are a part of a wider trend that has seen members of Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, protest in several European nations.

The wave of protest was triggered by students seeking education reform in France, with the standoff erupting in violence and looting two weeks ago.

For our standalone story on protests in France today, click here.

After a day of youth protests in Germany, senior police union representative Andreas Rosskopf said that there was no widespread property damage "so far."

"The Gen Z protests have turned out to be very peaceful," Rosskopf told the daily Rhenische Post.

While confrontations were reported after the marches ended in multiple cities, the people driving the clashes were "individuals acting independently, some of whom were masked."

Rosskopf, who represents Germany's federal police, said security forces acted very decisively and forcefully when such response was appropriate.

"Security forces remain absolutely ready to prevent any further clashes in the late evening of overnight," he said.

German security forces reported minor violent incidents in several cites in the wake of the Gen Z demonstrations.

In Hamburg, protesters at the city's Steintor square pelted the police with fireworks . Police used "immediate force" to clear the area, including using a water cannon.

Several police officers were injured during a similar incident in Frankfurt, according to a state interior minister.

Police also used a water cannon in Cologne, where the march was halted and turned into a stationary rally after some protesters covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

A police officers sustained light injuries in nearby Bonn during a confrontation with a group of protesters.

In Berlin, the authorities noted a rally separate from the official event organized by the Gen Z movement. Police initially reported "isolated instances of throwing eggs and bottles" from a crowd of around 500 people. The authorities later also reported "illegal burning of pyrotechnics" and said the crowd has grown to around 3,000 participants.

Several police officers were injured in a clash with a group of protesters following the Gen Z demonstration in Frankfurt, authorities said.

"One officers could be injured more seriously, but this will need some more looking into," said Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck.

"We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology," the state minister said.

"They have staged a massive attack against the police by throwing bottles, stones and fireworks."

Police responded with water cannons and have the situation in hand, he said

Thousands of young people took part in protests in 34 German cities on Saturday.

German Gen Z protesters called out rising living expenses, remilitarization of Germany, and declining education.

Some of the protesters also called for Germany's current chancellor, center-right Friedrich Merz, to step down.

The protests were held under the slogan Gen Z regelt (Gen Z sorts it).

Police were out in force after many politicians warned that Germany will not tolerate the kind of violence seen in France in mid-October.

Police reported incidents in which pepper spray and water cannon were used to keep crowds under control, with protesters setting off fireworks and lighting fires.

Most of the demonstrations ended peacefully.

But tensions remained high in some German cities with reports of several police officers injured.

In Germany's second-biggest city, Hamburg, police estimated 6,700 people taking part in the demonstration.

They reported some groups of black-clad protesters, some of whom also wore face masks, pulling apart construction site barriers and throwing them on the street. Some of the barriers were later set on fire.

Police said they pushed the crowd back and used pepper spray to break them apart. The fire was eventually put out.

Following an initial estimate of several hundred people attending the rally in central Berlin, police said that some 5,000 people were now gathered at the Brandenburg Gate. The organizers, "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z sorts it) gave a much higher number, saying 10,000 people were in attendance.

One of the speakers in Berlin, Kaja Schwab, decried false promises made by politicians.

The youth is being told that "we will do well if we work hard enough." In reality, the life is getting unaffordable and the young are "forced into military service," she said, in reference to Germany's renewed recruitment drive.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thousands of young people have joined the demonstrations in over 30 German cities, with police reporting largely peaceful protests.

Hundreds also gathered in Hamburg, Erfurt, Magdeburg, Dresden, Leipzig, Nuremberg, and elsehwere.

Retailers in several city centers had boarded up shop windows, particularly along luxury shopping streets, fearing unrest. Some shops were already closed for the Reformation Day public holiday.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available. More than 182,100 people had expressed interest in attending the events online.

Police in Cologne called off the planned "Gen Z regelt" procession after some participants covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.

"The demonstration will continue as a stationary rally," a police spokeswoman told the DPA news agency. Participants would remain on the Rhine riverbank, she said, appealing for restraint.

Attendance remained below the 15,000 people registered for the demonstration. Based on advance registrations, Cologne's protest was expected to be the largest in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Police repeatedly stopped a youth protest march in Stuttgart, citing participants covering their faces and leaving the agreed route.

Officers also reported smoke devices and firecrackers before the procession began. "Be loud, but remain peaceful," a police spokeswoman urged in a video.

In other German cities, police reported a largely peaceful start to demonstrations. Authorities estimated included 2,500 participants in Freiburg, more than 1,500 in Frankfurt, 1,200 in Mainz, 1,000 in Munich and 650 in Berlin.

No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available.

Politicians must involve young people in decision-making or risk the youth turning away from political institutions, education researcher Nina Kolleck warned.

Their exclusion "creates the impression that there is a policy for the old, but not for the young," the University of Potsdam professor told Germany's RBB Inforadio.

Kolleck pointed to decades of underinvestment in schools and the disproportionate impact of climate change on younger generations.

She warned that populist parties could exploit the resulting political vacuum if young people's frustrations continued to go unanswered.

Organizers of Germany's nationwide youth protests have accused the media of stoking fears of violence and distracting from their demands.

A "narrative of violence" was being used "to divert attention from our core demands," spokeswoman Veronika Dinter told the German broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.

She stressed that "GenZ regelt" — roughly meaning "Gen Z takes charge" — called for peaceful demonstrations, pointing to its published principles. Anyone who shared those principles was welcome, she said.

Dinter also regretted the decision by Germany's national school student representative body to distance itself from the protests. It had cited concerns including unclear organizational structures.

The initiative is holding rallies in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich, with local groups organizing protests in another 30 cities. Nearly 180,000 people had pledged online to attend, although actual turnout remained unclear.

Security authorities had warned that extremist groups could try to infiltrate the demonstrations.

People in Germany have the fundamental right, enshrined in the constitution or Basic Law, to assemble in public provided they remains peaceful and are unarmed.

However, several states have adopted their own assembly acts, which means some of them have additional restrictions, such as a ban on protesting on highways in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Federal law itself imposes the obligation on organizers of protests to notify the local authority entrusted with approving public assemblies at least 48 hours before they invite people publicly to take part.

This aims to allow authorities to put in place security measures and to lessen the impact of any assembly on others by, for example, instigating traffic control measures.

Spontaneous assemblies are, however, also allowed in cases where a topical issue of urgent importance is at stake, and there is no notification requirement for indoor assemblies.

Protests or other assemblies can be banned beforehand or dispersed while they are underway, but this is considered a means of last resort.

Some locations are also subject to restrictions on protests, such as the area around the Reichstag building in Berlin where the German parliament sits, and around the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.

Demonstrations around the Reichstag are, for example, permitted only when the parliament is not in session.

Post-war Germany has seen several massive demonstrations, including one in 1983, when 250,000 people — according to police estimates — gathered in the then West German capital, Bonn, to protest against the decision by NATO to station American nuclear missiles on German territory.

That was, however, surpassed in size by a protest in Berlin in 2003 against the invasion of Iraq by US-led forces, which drew a crowd of around half a million people.

There is some more detail on the law regarding the right of assembly in this DW article.

Young people are to take part in demonstrations across Germany on Saturday, following the example of their peers in France and other countries who have been calling for better educational prospects and future opportunities.

In Germany, organizers said there is also to be a focus on rejecting military conscription and on demanding more protection for the climate as the Earth warms, with potentially catastrophic effects.

Saturday's protests are being called for by the youth initiative "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") through a social media campaign

The group itself will directly organize four of the protests — in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich —, with associated demonstrations to take place in some 30 other cities.

It has explicitly called for peaceful protests without the violence that marred recent demonstrations in France.

This has not stopped several conservative politicians, notably from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), from warning that similar scenes could occur.

"Gen Z regelt" has, however, criticized what it sees as a wrong focus on the possibility of violence at the protests.

"It shows that our point about not being taken seriously or being heard is right. No one wants to work with us on the issues at stake but instead always put the topic of violence on the agenda," an organizer of the Munich protest told a press conference in Cologne.

However, other lawmakers have come out in support of the protests.

The leader of the parliamentary party of the Greens, Katharina Dröge, told the DPA news agency: "Young people are rightly furious because the federal government does not take their wishes seriously enough."

The Left Party leader, Luigi Pantisano, also said it was the right time for protests as the government mulls reforms of the nursing care and pensions systems, calling them "social cruelties."

"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1997 and 2012.

As Germany gears up for a day of mass youth protests, authorities in neighboring France are also bracing for new demonstrations on Saturday amid fears that the violence seen at October 17 rallies could repeat itself.

Some 70,000 police officers have been deployed to monitor around 150 protests across the country.

In recent weeks, protests by school pupils complaining about poor school conditions morphed into wider demonstrations on multiple issues, including the rising cost of living and social inequality.

On October 17 in particular, considerable violence occurred on the sidelines of mostly peaceful protests as extremists took the opportunity to plunder, riot and damage public property.

articles.title: Ukraine news: Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Kyiv-controlled territory
articles.body:
After Melania Trump reportedly brokered a localized truce, residents of Ukraine's Oleshky managed to leave the occupied city. Meanwhile, Kyiv claimed a hit on a Russian rocket fuel plant. DW has more.

Oleshky civilians arrive in Ukrainian territory from Belarus

Ukraine claims it hit a Russian plant producing solid fuel for rockets and missiles

Kyiv also reports strikes on military depots in occupied Ukrainian territory

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Istanbul for talks with Turkey's Recep Tayyip Erdogan

Here is a roundup of events from Russia's war in Ukraine on Saturday, October 31:

At a news conference after the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, DW correspondent Benjamin Alvarez Gruber asked German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul whether Sergey Lavrov's presence and the possibility of Russian President Vladimir Putin attending the G20 summit in Doral, Florida, in December signaled a normalization of relations with Russia.

Wadephul said the US and European countries were "on the same side."

"Speaking to the Russian Foreign Minister is not a concession we're making to Russia, but it is normal to speak," he said, adding that foreign ministers must be prepared to engage even with adversaries.

"You don't have to negotiate with partners, but you have to negotiate with somebody who has a different position and who's somehow also an adversary to freedom and to security in Europe. So it is necessary that we speak, and for that reason I think it was useful," Wadephul added.

The G20 foreign ministers skipped their traditional family photo at a meeting in Atlanta on Friday, amid objections from several European countries, Australia and Canada to appearing alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

Wadephul said: "We are not in a position that it was necessary or useful or a good idea to have a family photo because in the very situation we are in, Russia does not really show an interest to share our values and to share our interests."

The US State Department removed the photo from the agenda to prevent it from becoming a distraction or a spectacle.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Istanbul for talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, with Black Sea shipping among the issues on the agenda.

"We're working to strengthen the protection of our people, our bilateral partnership with Türkiye, and real diplomatic prospects," Zelenskyy wrote on X, using the alternative spelling for Turkey.

The Ukrainian president also plans to meet Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, the Istanbul-based Orthodox Christian leader.

The US embassy in Russia warned there was "a credible threat of a mass casualty event" at a historical site in southern Moscow.

"The US government is coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response," the US embassy in Moscow said in a post on X.

The alleged plot would target the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve, a sprawling complex of palaces and gardens built under the orders of Empress Cathrine the Great in the late 18th century.

Russia's federal law enforcement agency, the FSB, said it received the warning and was doing "appropriate work" in response to it, according to Russian news agencies.

Ukraine's military said it struck a factory producing solid rocket fuel in Russia's Rostov region, setting a warehouse ablaze and damaging four production workshops.

The attack on the Kamensky plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky involved drones and Neptune missiles, according to the Ukrainian account.

The military said the plant supplies fuel for ammunition used by Russia's Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as other missiles and air-launched weapons.

Ukraine also reported strikes on four Russian military supply depots in occupied parts of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Luhansk regions.

The claims have not been independently verified.

First evacuees from the Russian-occupied Oleshky have reached Ukrainian-controlled territory amid a localized ceasefire.

Oleshky, near the front line in the southern Kherson region, has been occupied by Russia since 2022. In recent weeks, the town has faced a severe humanitarian crisis.

Both sides have recently agreed to a localized ceasefire to extract the estimated 2,000 civilians still in Oleshky, down from its pre-invasion population of 24,000.

Moscow and Kyiv credited the US first lady, Melania Trump, with brokering the truce.

Residents were given a choice to go to Russia or travel via Belarus to the part of Ukraine controlled by Kyiv.

Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the initiative required "an enormous amount of work."

He said evacuees included a one-year-old baby and a 94-year-old resident of Oleshky. The evacuees brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon, according to Lubinets.

He expressed hope that the Oleshky arrangement can be replicated elsewhere.

The truce started on Tuesday and is due to end on Sunday night.

Welcome to DW's coverage of the latest developments in the Russian war on Ukraine.

You join us as Ukraine welcomes evacuees from Oleshky, a town in the Kherson region that has been occupied by Russia since 2022.

Meanwhile, Kyiv claimed it hit the Kamensky plant in the Rostov region deep inside Russia. The factory produces solid fuel for rockets and missiles.

Stay tuned for the latest news and analysis from the ongoing war.

articles.title: Germany news: Merkel calls for first female president
articles.body:
Former Chancellor Angela Merkel says it's time to consider a woman as Germany's next president. Meanwhile, Berlin's Left Party is deciding whether to enter coalition talks. DW has more.

Former Chancellor Angela Merkel calls for Germany's first female president

Several women are being discussed as possible successors to Frank-Walter Steinmeier, but no candidate has yet been agreed upon

Berlin's Left Party is expected to approve coalition talks with the Social Democrats and Greens, potentially paving the way for its first mayor

Delegates are meeting under tight security amid threats and planned protests

Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, October 31, 2026:

Youth protests have begun in cities across Germany, with demonstrators demanding better-funded schools, action on living costs and stronger climate protection. They also oppose a possible return to military conscription.

A railway crossing barrier just 46 centimeters (18 inches) long has become an unlikely selfie attraction in Cologne — but the city's transport operator says it serves a purpose.

The miniature arm stands beside tracks leading to a tram maintenance depot in the Weidenpesch district. It has even appeared on Google Maps as "Germany's smallest barrier."

Despite online mockery, it is no mistake. "It serves as a placeholder," said Cologne transport operator KVB spokesman Stephan Anemüller.

Installed in 2020, the barrier is to be extended once a planned cycle path is built alongside a nearby housing development. That avoids having to overhaul the crossing equipment later.

KVB is enjoying the attention. Anemüller called it "an amusing attraction" and said the operator would try to secure it a place in Cologne's city museum when it is eventually removed.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called for a woman to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, pointing out that no woman has held the office in the country's 77-year history.

Everyone should ask "whether it might finally be time," Merkel told MagentaTV.

She said she knew women capable of doing the job but declined to name anyone.

The Federal Convention elects Germany's next head of state on January 30. Steinmeier cannot seek a third consecutive term. The presidency is mostly a ceremonial role.

Bavarian parliamentary speaker Ilse Aigner has the backing of Markus Soder, leader of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU).

Other names being discussed include Bundestag president Julia Klockner, Education Minister Karin Prien and former Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer, all from Merkel's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Merkel described the debate as "strange" and criticized its "unpleasant undertone."

She also challenged her party's direction, saying the CDU's identity went beyond economic policy. "The CDU was always about building bridges to all parts of society — and that must be brought back to the forefront."

Berlin's socialist Left Party is expected to approve coalition negotiations with the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and environmentalist Greens, potentially paving the way for the city's first Left Party mayor.

The SPD and Greens have already backed talks, which could begin on Monday. But the Left Party's youth wing opposes the alliance, calling instead for a "strong socialist opposition."

Delegates gathered under tight security in Berlin's Lichtenberg district following calls for protests accusing the party of betraying voters. Its candidate for mayor, Elif Eralp, has been given personal protection.

The Left Party won September's election with 25.7% of the vote. The governing coalition of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and SPD lost its majority.

If the three parties reach a deal, Eralp, currently the Left Party's parliamentary leader in Berlin, could become the city's next governing mayor.

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

Germany has never had a woman as its head of state. Former Chancellor Angela Merkel thinks it might be time to change that.

Merkel, who was Germany's first female chancellor, has called for a woman to succeed President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

Meanwhile, could Berlin be heading for its first mayor from the socialist Left Party?

Stay with us here for these stories and more of what Germany is talking about today.

articles.title: India news: Amit Shah challenges Rahul Gandhi to debate vote theft in parliament
articles.body:
Home Minister Amit Shah has challenged Rahul Gandhi to debate electoral irregularity allegations in parliament, ahead of a major opposition rally against the election chief in Delhi.

These updates are closed. These were top headlines from India on Saturday, October 31:

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Friday challenged opposition leaders Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav to discuss allegations of electoral irregularities in parliament, even as the opposition geared for a major rally against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar , according to media reports.

"I am ready to call a special session of Parliament to discuss vote theft allegations," Shah said, accusing the opposition of making baseless allegations against the Election Commission and staging protests while skirting parliamentary debate.

His remarks came as the opposition INDIA bloc prepared to hold a symbolic "public impeachment" of Kumar on Saturday, followed by a major rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on November 1.

Around 30 speakers from 21 opposition parties are expected to participate.

The opposition is demanding Kumar's resignation over his role in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the scrapping of the SIR, alleging that the exercise could disenfranchise voters and benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

In a call for the November 1 rally, Rahul Gandhi said "anyone who cares about democracy must come."

"The vote is yours. The fight is also yours," the Congress leader wrote on X.

Earlier, the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) also threw their weight behind the rally saying the movement would lend its support to any organization fighting for free and fair elections in India, including the opposition alliance.

A German citizen was among two people killed in a suspected electrocution at a five-star hotel swimming pool in Bengaluru on Friday evening, media reports said.

The 57-year-old German national and another 45-year-old man from Slovakia had gone swimming at the Conrad Hotel when the incident occurred, according to reports.

A US tourist and an Indian hotel employee were also injured while attempting to rescue the victims.

Their conditions are stable and expected to be discharged soon, reports said.

The hotel management said it was cooperating with local authorities and that the cause of the incident had not yet been established.

India will conduct its next population census from January 25 to February 28, 2027, followed by a revision exercise from March 1 to 5, according to a gazette notification issued on Friday cited by the Indian Express newspaper.

According to authorities, the option for self-enumeration would be available from January 10 to 24, ahead of the door-to-door exercise.

The census will cover all states and Union territories except Manipur, Goa, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Ladakh and snow-bound areas of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir, which will follow separate schedules, the report said.

Students of Jamia Millia Islamia university in New Delhi held a victory march on campus on Friday, after the university administration agreed to reinstate the student union and set a timeline for elections.

The university agreed to restore its students' union and hold elections after nearly two decades, following an 18-day hunger strike by students demanding its reinstatement.

Tensions escalated last week when police allegedly detained protesters, with some students also accusing personnel of assaulting them.

Under a formal order issued by the administration, the university has committed to finalizing and implementing the union's constitution by May 15, 2027.

Student union elections will be held within six weeks of the commencement of the next academic session.

The Jamia Millia Islamia Students' Union (JMISU) was disbanded in 2006.

On Friday, Delhi experienced temperatures more typical of a winter day than an October afternoon.

Delhi recorded its lowest October daytime temperature in 75 years on Friday, with a maximum temperature of 20.7 degrees Celsius, which more than 10 degrees below normal, PTI news agency reported, citing data from the India Meteorological Department (IMD).

The low temperature came after two days of persistent rainfall.

The maximum temperature at Safdarjung, Delhi's base weather station, was the lowest for October since records began in 1951, the IMD data added.

Delhi also recorded its wettest October day in four years, receiving 61.4 mm of rainfall in the 24 hours ending Friday morning.

The rainfall also helped clean up air pollution levels, with the Indian capital's notoriously bad Air Quality Index (AQI) improving to a "satisfactory" reading of 60.

However, experts say pollution levels could deteriorate to the "poor" category on November 1 and remain poor or very poor over the coming days.

India's space agency successfully launched a navigation satellite on Friday night to strengthen the country's indigenous alternative to GPS.

The NVS-03 satellite, the third in Indian Space Research Organisation's (ISRO) next-generation navigation series, was carried into orbit by the "GSLV-F18" rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, located on an island in the Bay of Bengal.

According to ISRO the "the GSLV-F18 vehicle placed NVS-03 satellite into a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit."

An earlier statement by the agency said the satellite is "intended to augment the NavIC constellation and support continuity of navigation services."

It is designed to provide navigation coverage across India and up to 1,500 kilometers (932 miles) beyond its borders.

NavIC is seen as an alternative to the Global Positioning System (GPS) system owned by the United States government and developed to reduce India's dependence on foreign navigation systems.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi celebrated the successful launch as a "great accomplishment."

An oil tanker carrying 27 Indian seafarers was targeted with limpet mines in the Strait of Hormuz.A small boat attached two mines to the vessel's hull, causing a fire in the engine room, maritime security sources said on Friday.

Indian Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal said all Indian seafarers aboard the vessel were safe and had sustained no injuries. Sonowal also added that two Indians aboard another tanker that faced a separate attack on October 29 were also safe.

The attack on the Panama-flagged Louise 1 occurred on Thursday, around 25 nautical miles (46 km) northeast of Oman's Khasab.

The fire was extinguished, the crew was safe and there was no environmental impact, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said.

The incident marks the first known successful use of limpet mines against a vessel in the waterway since the US-Iran war began in February.

The identity of those behind the attacks was not immediately known.

The Strait of Hormuz,a vital chokepoint for oil and gas transport, is seeing attacks on ships at the highest level since the Iran war began, according to US-based think tank Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

Incidentally, the Louise 1 was hit earlier with naval drones in the Black Sea by Ukrainian forces over its alleged role in transporting Russian oil and being part of the so-called shadow fleet of tankers deployed by Moscow.

This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi studio bringing you the top updates from across India on the last day of the coldest October in 75 years. Brrr…must be true!

On a more serious note, two vessels with Indian crew members were attacked in the Strait of Hormuz in the past two days. Thankfully, the Indian government has said all sailors were safe.

Meanwhile, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) successfully launched the NVS-03 satellite to strengthen its indigenous navigation system and reduce reliance on the US-owned GPS.
