articles.title: 5 state Supreme Court races to watch on Tuesday
articles.body:
by Sophie Brams 10/31/26 05:00 PM ET

Voters in half of the country will decide who sits on the bench of their state’s highest court next Tuesday.

State Supreme Court races are on ballot in two dozen states this November, with partisan, nonpartisan and retention contests determining which candidates win seats or remain on the bench of courts that often have the final word on interpreting state law in consequential matters like abortion and redistricting.

“State Supreme Court is a super important level of the ballot for us because so much of people’s rights and liberties is now determined at the state level,” said Deirdre Schifeling, the chief political and advocacy officer for the ACLU, which has spent about $5.5 million on voter outreach efforts in Michigan, Montana and North Carolina.

And while the ideological balance of power isn’t up for grabs in most states, experts say what happens next week could set the stage for shifts in 2028 and beyond.

Here are five races to watch on election night:

In Michigan, six candidates are running for two seats on the state’s Supreme Court.

Chief Justice Megan Cavanagh is seeking another eight-year term, and Justice Noah Hood is seeking his first full term. Hood was appointed to the high court by Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) after former Chief Justice Elizabeth Clement retired in 2025.

All of the candidates will be placed on the same ballot, which also includes contenders Michael Warren, Casandra Morse-Bills, Thomas Howe and Jody White in an open election where the top two vote-getters will be declared winners.

The Wolverine State uses a unique method to determine which names make it on the general election ballot. Political parties select candidates during nominating conventions, but the elections are technically nonpartisan, so those party labels are not listed.

It’s no secret which way each candidate leans politically.

Cavanagh and Hood are Democratic Party nominees, while lower court judges Morse-Bills and Warren were nominated by Republicans.

Howe and White were both nominated by the U.S. Taxpayers Party, the state affiliate of the ultraconservative Constitution Party. The Michigan Advance reports that neither is licensed to practice law in Michigan, a requirement for any judge or justice in the state court system.

Recent election cycles have helped shore up liberals’ 6-1 advantage on the Michigan Supreme Court, with only one Republican-backed justice currently on the bench.

Both Democratic incumbents losing their reelection bids would tighten those margins but keep the majority intact.

A Democratic appointee in Missouri is running to keep his seat on the state’s high court — but he has no opponent.

Justice Paul Wilson, who was appointed to the Missouri Supreme Court bench in 2012, is facing a retention vote. That’s an up-and-down vote to decide whether an incumbent keeps their job.

There isn’t a power balance at stake, as justices appointed by Republican governors hold a 5-2 edge on the bench. But it remains to be seen whether a mid-decade redistricting fight that ran through the Supreme Court will have any bearing on voters.

Wilson authored the dissenting opinion in a narrow March decision that found the GOP-controlled legislature could redraw congressional lines before the next U.S. census.

In September he joined with colleagues on a unanimous decision that invalidated a 7-1 House map that sought to dismantle Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) district and hand Republicans a pickup opportunity in the midterms. The court ruled that the new lines, which had been used for the primaries, could not be implemented until voters weighed in on a general election referendum.

The battle made to the U.S. Supreme Court three times, with the GOP losing each round.

The Missouri Judicial Performance Review Committee, an independent, statewide panel that evaluates the performance of judges for retention, has recommended that Wilson should be retained.

It is rare for judges to lose retention elections. Wilson earned 63 percent yes votes the last time he was on the ballot, according to state election results.

The race to replace a retiring justice on the Montana Supreme Court is a rematch between two lower court judges.

Flathead County judges Amy Eddy and Dan Wilson are running to succeed outgoing Justice Beth Baker, who is stepping down after 16 years on the bench.

The pair have already faced each other once this year, with Eddy securing just over 7,600 more votes than Wilson in the June primary. As the only two candidates on the ballot, both advanced to the general election.

It’s officially a nonpartisan contest — meaning no party labels appear alongside their names — but that hasn’t stopped it from becoming something of a proxy battle.

The Montana GOP has lined up behind Wilson, hosting him as the keynote speaker at the state party’s winter kickoff event in February.

“I call myself a constitutional Conservative because I decide cases based on the facts and not feelings, principles above all else, and the Constitution,” Wilson said at the time, according to Montana Public Radio.

Eddy, meanwhile, has picked up endorsements from labor unions and environmental groups like the Montana Conservation Voters.

“When Montana constitutionalised environmental protections, it did so with the understanding that courts would serve as a forum where those rights were taken seriously, interpreted faithfully, and enforced when necessary,” Eddy said in a statement shared by the group.

Outside groups have spent a combined roughly $2.25 million in the contest, according to TV advertising data compiled by the Brennan Center for Justice.

In addition to electing a state Supreme Court justice, voters are also weighing a ballot measure that would enshrine nonpartisan judicial elections in the state constitution after the GOP-controlled legislature tried unsuccessfully to advance bills that would have made them partisan.

“We believe that there is an effort underway in Montana at the state legislative level to make state supreme courts partisan as a way to eventually elect Republican, hard right judges who will then take away reproductive rights,” said Schifeling.

The court currently has a 4-3 liberal lean, though experts note that Baker has sometimes acted as a swing vote. That leaves room for a potential ideological flip if Wilson emerges on top.

The outcome could prove even more important in 2028, when two state Supreme Court seats will be up for election.

A lot of eyes — and money — is also on North Carolina, where Democratic incumbent Justice Anita Earls is defending her seat against former Republican state lawmaker Sarah Stevens.

It’s the only seat up for election on the state Supreme Court this Tuesday, but it’s one that both parties have their eyes on looking ahead to 2028.

Republicans won a majority on the Tar Heel State’s top court in the 2022 midterms and, within months, reversed the court’s own prior rulings that had struck down a voter ID law and redistricting maps as unconstitutional.

The 2022 results followed years of wrangling between the GOP and Democrats over how the state’s judicial elections should be held. Those races were partisan for much of the 20th century, but after Republicans started winning more in the late 1990s and early 2000s, Democratic lawmakers removed party labels from the ballot.

State Supreme Court elections remained that way until 2016, when the Republican-controlled legislature changed them back to partisan after liberals secured a one-seat majority.

The contests have largely fallen along the state’s broader political lines since then, and conservatives now have a 5-2 edge.

A win for Stevens would expand that advantage, while Democrats are hoping Earls can cling to her seat to avoid shrinking the minority even further. Democratic incumbent Allison Riggs barely won reelection two years ago in a hotly contested election by less than 1,000 votes.

Tuesday’s race has attracted millions of dollars, with figures from the Brennan Center showing Earls has spent just shy of $4.2 million. North Carolina Families First, a left-leaning PAC, also launched a multimillion advertising blitz targeting Stevens.

The implications for 2028 are potentially big. Three sitting Republican justices are up for election that cycle, and at least one has already said he won’t seek another term.

Five of the nine seats on the Washington Supreme Court are up for election.

Chief Justice Debra Stephens is facing attorney Todd Bloom in her bid for another six-year term. Stephens has been on the bench since 2008.

Justice Theo Angelis and Justice Colleen Melody, both of whom were tapped by Gov. Bob Ferguson (D) to fill vacancies on the court this year, are seeking to finish out the remainder of the terms. They are being challenged by retired Federal Way Municipal Court Judge Dave Larson and attorney Scott Edwards, respectively.

The remaining two races are for seats left open by justices who opted not to seek re-election. King County Superior Court Judge Sean O’Donnell is squaring off against appellate Judge Ian Birk for one of those seats, while Mason County Superior Court Judge David Stevens is running against King County Superior Judge Jaime Hawk for the other.

Experts aren’t anticipating a major ideological shift in this cycle, but the officially nonpartisan races are still attracting plenty of attention.

The state Republican Party is backing attorney Edwards, Larson and Bloom in their bids to unseat the sitting justices. It has also endorsed Stevens and O’Donnell for the open seats.

Various Democratic officials and left-leaning groups like Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates have signaled their support for the three incumbents, as well as Birk and Hawk.

But it’s not a clean partisan split. O’Donnell has also picked up endorsements from some Democrats, according to his campaign.

The interest comes as the court is expected to take up major issues in the coming months, according to the Washington State Standard, including reforms to bail bond policy and a challenge to the state’s new income tax on high earners.

An initiative to repeal the tax is also on the ballot.

articles.title: Lula and Milei both owe their victories to Trump
articles.body:
by Imran Khalid, opinion contributor 10/31/26 03:00 PM ET

Argentina President Javier Milei and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva agree on almost nothing. But they now share a debt to President Trump.

A year ago this week, Milei’s party won Argentina’s midterms after Washington tied a $20 billion rescue to the result. On Sunday, Lula won a fourth term in Brazil after more than a year of American tariffs and sanctions bound up with the fate of the Bolsonaro family. Only one of the two was supposed to benefit.

The quick reading of Brazil’s result is that Trump’s push for friendly governments in Latin America has hit a wall. That reading gets his record wrong. Since returning to office, Trump has endorsed, funded or threatened his way into at least seven foreign elections, and the results follow a pattern. When he arrives as a patron, offering something voters need, his candidates win. When he arrives as a punisher of the whole country, or as a cheerleader with nothing concrete to offer, they lose.

Start with the patron. “If he loses, we are not going to be generous with Argentina,” Trump said with Milei beside him at the White House. Milei’s party took 40.8 percent. In Honduras, Trump warned that Washington would not be “throwing good money after bad” if Nasry Asfura lost. Asfura won by less than a point. In Poland, Trump received Karol Nawrocki in the Oval Office, and his Homeland Security secretary suggested that U.S. military ties could deepen with Nawrocki as president. Nawrocki won narrowly. In Colombia, where Washington had already sanctioned the president, Trump endorsed Abelardo de la Espriella, who won a runoff so close that his rival demanded a recount.

Every one of those wins was narrow. In a close race, a credible offer is enough.

Then the punisher. In Canada, Trump’s tariffs and talk of a 51st state erased a Conservative lead of double digits and returned the Liberals under Mark Carney, who told voters Trump wanted “to break us so America can own us.” In Brazil, Washington imposed 50 percent tariffs in July 2025, citing the prosecution of former President Jair Bolsonaro. He revoked the visas of eight Supreme Court justices and sanctioned the judge who led the case. This July it added a 25 percent tariff, with Marco Rubio blaming Lula’s “ego.” On the eve of Sunday’s vote, Reuters reported that two State Department officials had pushed sanctions meant to tilt the election toward the Bolsonaros.

Brazil’s two leading pollsters had Flávio Bolsonaro, Jair’s son, ahead 51-49 percent the day before the vote. He lost by 4.4 million votes. The most telling choice of his campaign was his own: five months after sitting in the Oval Office with Trump, he declined to seek Trump’s endorsement for the runoff. Lula closed by declaring that Brazil “will not accept being anyone’s backyard.”

The third role is the cheerleader. Trump gave Viktor Orbán his “Complete and Total Endorsement,” Vice President JD Vance flew to Budapest to campaign, and Hungarians were promised prosperity if Orbán won. His Fidesz party took 37.8 percent. Péter Magyar’s Tisza won 53.6 percent and 138 of 199 seats, running against corruption and for mended ties with the European Union. Asked about it afterward, Trump said, “I wasn’t that involved.”

Sort the cases and a rule emerges. A conditional offer turns an election into a transaction, and voters in a country short of dollars, aid or protection can price it. A punishment aimed at the whole nation turns the same election into a referendum on who runs the country, and the candidate who stands up to Washington wins it. An endorsement with nothing concrete behind it, in a country whose real patron sits elsewhere, is noise. Voters abroad will take Washington’s money. They will not take its orders.

Brazil shows why punishment fails against a country with options. China bought 28.7 percent of Brazil’s exports in 2025; the United States bought 10.8 percent. Under the tariffs, shipments to America fell 35.4 percent year on year in October 2025, and Lula could still tell the U.N. General Assembly last month that exports were at a record. A country that can absorb a penalty has no reason to obey it. Its voters have every reason to resent it.

None of this means Washington decided these elections alone. Colombians voted on fear of armed groups, Hungarians on corruption, Brazilians on prices and pensions, and Lula’s campaign brought nearly 3 million more voters to the polls between rounds. But elections are won at the margin, and Honduras was settled by fewer than one vote in a hundred. In races that close, an American offer or an American threat becomes the frame through which the last undecided voter makes up their mind.

The lesson Washington is likeliest to draw from Brazil is the convenient one: pay, don’t punish. The trouble is what that policy does to the world’s democracies. It sorts them into two classes, those dependent enough to be bought and those independent enough to be provoked. The first will keep electing Washington’s friends by thin margins and on Washington’s terms. The second will keep rewarding leaders who run against it. Neither produces the kind of ally that holds when it matters.

The next test is France, which chooses a president in April 2027. When a court convicted Marine Le Pen of embezzlement last year, Trump answered with a post that ended “FREE MARINE LE PEN!” She is now cleared to run. France is no Argentina: Washington has no rescue to offer it, and no penalty French voters would quietly accept. If the pattern holds, the most useful thing Trump can do for Le Pen is stay away from her campaign. Brazilians showed on Sunday what his help costs.

Imran Khalid is a physician and has a master’s degree in international relations.

articles.title: Evacuees from Russia-controlled Oleshky arrive back in Ukraine amid U.S.-brokered ceasefire
articles.body:
by Sarah Davis 10/31/26 01:22 PM ET

Residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday amid a localized U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement.

The halt in fighting, which was secured earlier this month by first lady Melania Trump, went into effect on Tuesday and is set to last through Saturday.

Residents were given the choice of being transported to Russia, Ukraine or remaining in the city with replenished food supplies. Those who chose to return to Ukraine were transported through Russia and Belarus before reaching the country’s Chernihiv region on Saturday.

The city, which is located in the Russian-controlled Kherson region, has faced shortages in food, medicine and other vital supplies amid the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war. Around 2,000 people were reportedly trapped in the city, including a large elderly population.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked the first lady for her efforts to secure the localized ceasefire in a Saturday social media post announcing the return of the Oleshky evacuees to Ukraine.

“As of now, Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky have crossed the Ukrainian border in the Chernihiv region,” he wrote. “All of them will receive the assistance they need. It is important that government agencies and all the regional and local authorities involved work effectively and help our people adapt.”

Zelensky expressed his hope that humanitarian access to the city would “remain open.”

Melania Trump responded on social media Saturday to a video shared by a Ukrainian official of the moment the residents reached Ukraine.

“Oleshky proves we can raise humanity above war,” she wrote. “Together, we can build a peaceful planet, a world of promise for our children.”

On Friday, the first lady said the humanitarian convoy effort, which included 25 buses and 50 medical professionals, could safely evacuate 750 people from the city.

“All elements of the convoy, including the safe passageway in and out of Oleshky, was established through mutual agreement between Russian and Ukrainian leaders,” she wrote in a social media post.

José Andrés, the founder of World Central Kitchen, said his nonprofit team had set up food supplies in preparation for the evacuees’ arrival back in Ukraine.

“The route was long: from Oleshky through Crimea to Anapa in Russia, then a flight to Belarus and onward by road into Chernihiv region. After a journey like that, warm, good food matters a great deal,” Andrés wrote on social media, alongside a video of evacuees going through a food line.

Zelensky praised the nonprofit’s assistance and said he was “proud and grateful” for Andrés’s involvement in this effort.

“Thank you to you and the entire World Central Kitchen team for the warmth of your dishes and hearts,” the Ukrainian leader wrote in a social media post.

articles.title: Iran’s Supreme Leader threatens US with response if strikes are launched after midterms
articles.body:
by Sarah Davis 10/31/26 11:51 AM ET

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued a stark message on Friday, warning the U.S. against its reported plans to resume strikes against the country following the midterm elections.

Khamenei directed senior Iranian military officials in a meeting to deliver an “immediate, impactful response without geographical limitations,” according to Iran’s official IRNA news agency.

The leader reportedly instructed these military leaders to update their target database “to ensure that all physical and non-physical assets” of the U.S. and Israeli armies are brought within reach of the Iranian armed forces.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

On Friday, several outlets reported that the U.S. had notified several Arab countries to prepare for a short U.S. military campaign following the Nov. 3 elections, with fresh attacks expected as soon as the following day, three senior Gulf Arab officials told MS NOW.

President Trump promised earlier this month he would not launch strikes against Iran ahead of the midterms, as he continues to face pressure to wind down this war amid rising energy prices and other costs tied to the conflict.

The war, which began with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes launched on Feb. 28, has now stretched over eight months. The conflict has cost the U.S. around $47 billion, according to an Oct. 16 estimate from U.S. Central Command.

At a rally last week, the president indicated his administration “may do another little Epic Fury” if Iran refuses to meet U.S. demands, in reference to the U.S.’s military operations against Tehran, dubbed “Operation Epic Fury.”

“If they’re smart, they’ll just say, ‘Let’s get down to business,’” the president said. “But, you know, I doubt they’ll do that because perhaps they’re not smart.”

The Trump administration has also waged a massive effort to isolate Iran’s economy, called “Operation Economic Outcast,” by placing sanctions on Iranian oil and imposing a U.S. naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil trading corridor.

The Treasury Department said in a Friday report that the campaign was “decimating” Iran’s economy, finding headline inflation in the country reached 90 percent in September.

articles.title: DC, Virginia sue to block Trump’s triumphal arch
articles.body:
by Ford McCracken 10/31/26 10:43 AM ET

Washington, D.C., and Virginia sued the National Parks Service and Interior Department to block President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch on Saturday, a new court filing shows.

The planned arch would resemble arches in other cities, including Paris’s Arc de Triomphe, and be constructed on the border between D.C. and Virginia.

In the court filing, the plaintiffs call the arch “flagrantly unlawful” because Trump did not seek congressional authorization to construct the project.

“In their rush to break ground on the Arch, Defendants have made only half-hearted gestures at complying with these requirements,” the lawsuit reads. “Perhaps recognizing that the project is legally indefensible, Defendants have made clear that they will attempt to outrun judicial review.”

The president has pushed forward with his efforts to renovate Washington despite frequent lawsuits and a lack of congressional authorization. One particular case involved the White House ballroom, in which the East Wing was demolished and construction on the ballroom began immediately.

When sued over the project, the Supreme Court ruled in the Trump administration’s favor after Trump argued the ballroom construction needed to continue for national security purposes.

The plaintiffs in Saturday’s lawsuit say they hope to avoid a similar situation with the arch.

“It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue—as they have done in other cases—that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” the lawsuit reads.

In a statement to The Hill, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones called the project “an affront” to Arlington National Cemetery, where the arch would be located.

“President Trump’s illegal vanity project is an affront to this hallowed ground and the extraordinary sacrifices it represents,” Jones said. “The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place.”

D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb said the lawsuit was filed to prevent “irreparable harm” to the District.

“Construction of the Arch is flagrantly illegal and will cause serious, immediate, and irreparable harm to the District and its residents,” Schwalb said in a statement to The Hill. “We’re filing this lawsuit now to protect DC’s unique interests and critical role in preserving the safeguards that keep our nation’s capital beautiful and safe.”

The Parks Service did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The proposals for the arch at one point included military plans, as Trump said it would be used for snipers and drones, though the final plans submitted to the city did not include the military complex.

Arlington County, Va. previously sued the Trump administration to block the arch in early October.

articles.title: Federal appeals court lifts Idaho ruling permitting abortions for women’s health
articles.body:
by Sarah Davis 10/31/26 10:28 AM ET

A federal appeals court paused a judge’s earlier ruling that ordered Idaho to allow exceptions to its abortion ban in cases where a doctor deemed it necessary to protect the mother’s health.

In a 2-1 decision issued on Friday, the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a doctor who sued over the state’s ban was unlikely to prevail on claims that the right to a health-saving abortion is constitutional.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in its 2022 Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization decision there was no constitutional right to abortion, overturning its landmark 1973 Roe v. Wade decision.

Idaho and a dozen other states issued near-total abortion bans following the high court’s ruling. Abortion is restricted in an additional nine states, according to the Center for Reproductive Rights.

The appeals court’s pause applies to an 81-page decision issued by U.S. District Judge Lynn Winmill in August, which the federal judge later limited to bar the state law’s enforcement against the plaintiff, Stacey Seyb.

“We think it unlikely that Dr. Seyb will be able to square the district court’s perspective on the history and tradition concerning abortions with the Supreme Court’s perspective in Dobbs,” the appeals court said in its decision.

Circuit Judges Kim Wardlaw and Consuelo Callahan made up the court’s majority in this ruling. Wardlaw, a Clinton appointee, issued a concurring opinion, in which she noted that the appeals court was “bound by the decisions of the Supreme Court.”

“As such, in light of the Dobbs majority opinion, I join Judge Callahan in concluding that Defendants have shown a likelihood of success on the merits,” Wardlaw continued.

In a dissenting opinion, Circuit Judge Marsha Berzon found the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision applied only to elective abortions and warned that some women could be “required to continue their pregnancies at serious, permanent risk to their health” because of this ruling.

“The risk, absent the injunction, to Dr. Seyb’s pregnant patients of serious and lasting harm short of death is definitionally a risk of irreparable injury,” she wrote.

articles.title: Alaska’s decoy scandal brings back the usual suspects for shady election tactics
articles.body:
by Jonathan Turley, opinion contributor 10/31/26 10:00 AM ET

Marc Elias is back. The notorious Democratic lawyer who played a critical role in the 2016 Russia hoax is again in the news. His law firm has been identified by the New York Times as part of the expanding scandal involving Democratic effort to confuse voters in Alaska with a decoy candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan.

For those familiar with Elias’s checkered history, this is a case of rounding up the usual suspects.

The scandal involving Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has quickly snowballed this week. A New York Times blockbuster investigative report quotes former staff who claim she knew of a cynical effort by her own campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to confuse voters by recruiting and fielding a decoy “Dan Sullivan” candidate in the race against incumbent Sen. Daniel S. Sullivan (R-Alaska). State and federal investigations are now unfolding, with dozens of federal subpoenas raining down on Alaska.

The effort to get voters to cast mistaken ballots is grossly unethical and, even in these rage-filled times, a uniquely disgraceful scheme. Peltola and the Democratic Party had long denied any involvement in the other Sullivan’s candidacy. So when the Times produced evidence that she allegedly knew, and that Democratic staffers and lawyers had been deeply involved from the beginning, many of us were surprised — that is, until the name “Marc Elias” emerged. Then it made more sense.

The Elias Law Group was already in the news this election cycle for threatening reporters with defamation lawsuits if they kept asking questions about the health of former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for Senate in North Carolina. Earlier, Elias caused a stir during an unsuccessful Democratic gerrymandering effort, raising the idea that Democratic leaders could abolish the entire Virginia government after courts blocked their attempted radical redistricting plan.

The fact that figures such as Peltola and Cooper wanted to be associated with any law firm headed by Elias is itself an indictment of their judgment and standards.

Despite his losses in cases such as National Republican Senatorial Committee v. Federal Election Commission, Elias is still a favorite of many on the left thanks to his aggression and partisan fervor. The controversies that make him notorious to many make him popular with others.

Elias was the general counsel to the Clinton presidential campaign when it secretly funded the infamous Steele Dossier and pushed the false Alfa Bank conspiracy theory. (His fellow Perkins Coie partner, Michael Sussmann, was later indicted but acquitted for making a false statement to the FBI.)

Clinton campaign officials lied to reporters during the 2016 campaign, denying any involvement in the Steele Dossier. Journalists discovered the truth after the election — that the Clinton campaign had hidden payments for the dossier as “legal fees” among the $5.6 million paid to Perkins Coie. New York Times reporter Ken Vogel said that when tried to report the story, Elias “pushed back vigorously, saying ‘You (or your sources) are wrong.’”

Times reporter Maggie Haberman later observed that “Folks involved in funding this lied about it, and with sanctimony, for a year.” The Federal Election Commission ultimately sanctioned the Clinton campaign for the subterfuge.

While raising money as the self-proclaimed defenders of democracy, Elias’s group has been involved in gerrymandering and efforts criticized as seeking to invalidate Republican votes, including unsuccessful efforts to challenge Democratic electoral losses.

In Maryland, Elias’s team supported another abusive gerrymandering scheme that a court found not only violated Maryland law but the state constitution’s equal protection, free speech and free elections clauses. The court found that the proposed map “subverts the will of those governed.”

One media site accused Elias and his group of “making millions off gerrymandering efforts” while publicly denouncing Republican gerrymandering.

In 2024, Elias’s legal team was also accused of pushing “to bar third-party presidential candidates — including Cornel West — from swing state ballots where they might siphon votes” from Democratic nominee Kamala Harris.

Likewise, the New York Times reported that the Elias firm’s work “on behalf of a Soros-funded PAC in Texas … was opposed by a left-leaning election watchdog as undermining laws intended to limit the influence of major donors.”

His group’s work for New York’s redistricting effort was ridiculed as not only ignoring the express will of the voters and also effectively negating Republicans’ votes.

In 2024, the Chief Judge of the Western District of Wisconsin criticized the Elias Law Group for one of its challenges. Judge James Peterson (an Obama appointee) said that the argument “simply does not make any sense.”

Now, Elias’s group is linked to the decoy scandal in Alaska, which allegedly aimed to make voters cast mistaken ballots. What distinguishes lawyers involved in this type of voter disruption is less their talent as their willingness. There are simply some things that most lawyers will not do.

There is also a difference in how lawyers are treated in such controversies. It often seems that in election controversies involving Republican lawyers are more likely to end with bar charges and disbarments. Take John Eastman, the former Trump lawyer disbarred in California after a state bar panel found that he had pushed unfounded legal theories and conspired to obstruct the electoral vote count on Jan. 6, 2021.

Although I publicly disagreed with Eastman’s theories, I opposed the effort to disbar him as setting a dangerous precedent for lawyers seeking to advance novel or unpopular theories of recovery or liability. After all, lawyers on the left routinely advance dubious theories, including some that are more ideologically than legally driven. Such controversies rarely rise to the level of disbarment, especially when more appropriate sanctions are available, ranging from reprimands to fines.

Eastman is currently asking the Supreme Court to overturn his disbarment. It is unlikely that Elias Law Group or Peltola’s lawyers will face similar disbarment efforts — nor should they, in my view, unless they were involved in criminal conduct. But the disparate treatment afforded to counsel in this country by party remains a growing concern. What draws a shower of bar complaints for Republican lawyers brings a windfall of clients for Democratic lawyers.

The New York Times has produced sources alleging that lawyers for Peltola’s campaign were involved in this effort, even though they previously told a federal court that they “lack knowledge or information” and “deny any allegation about those purposes.” Such filings and statements could raise ethical or even criminal questions in investigations at both the state and federal levels.

Meanwhile, though, tens of thousands of voters in Alaska have already cast ballots that included the decoy Sullivan candidate. This could result in a nasty fight in Congress if Peltola prevails in the vote count. And when it happens, that is where we will find Marc Elias in his element.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution.”

articles.title: Trump administration attempts to bypass restrictions on sending Afghan refugees to Afghanistan: Reports
articles.body:
by Sarah Davis 10/31/26 09:26 AM ET

The Trump administration is proceeding with plans to effectively deport some Afghan refugees to Afghanistan, despite concerns they could become targets of the Taliban there, according to several reports.

Dozens of Afghan immigrants have been detained in Louisiana and over 150 people are expected to be deported, making this among the largest single deportations of Afghans, according to The New York Times.

The U.S. is restricted from sending refugees straight to Afghanistan, as the country lacks diplomatic relations with the Taliban. Instead, the Trump administration plans to send the group to Pakistan, where they are widely expected to be sent to Afghanistan.

The Department of Homeland Security told The Hill in a statement on Saturday that “ICE does not comment on prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details.”

“For operational security reasons and the safety of our officers, we would not confirm future removal operations,” DHS continued in their statement.

Bloomberg was the first to report on the initial details of this plan earlier this week, citing a government official with knowledge of the plans.

The deportation flight to Pakistan could depart as soon as Monday morning, according to NBC News.

In the past, the U.S. has deported some Afghans to Afghanistan through intermediary countries, but these cases have involved immigrants with terrorism or other serious criminal charges.

This is the latest in the Trump administration’s efforts to carry out a widespread deportation campaign across the country.

President Trump blocked the admission of Afghans and other refugees, and his administration has deported thousands of people to countries where they have no ties. The Supreme Court is set to rule on the legality of these third-country deportations this term.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, slammed this latest deportation plan in a statement shared to social media on Friday.

“It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan – who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this,” Shaheen said.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who sits on the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, similarly criticized the move.

“We made a promise to our Afghan allies—that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them,” he wrote in a social media post. “This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death.”

articles.title: El-Sayed accuses Stevens of ‘relitigating’ primary after calls for apology on Israel
articles.body:
by Ford McCracken 10/31/26 08:05 AM ET

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) is firing back on his former primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), after she expected him to apologize over his comments on Israel just a few days out from the high-stakes Michigan Senate race.

Stevens said would appear alongside El-Sayed for the first time since their August primary this weekend but criticized him over his response to a controversial anti-Israel ad that appeared to link the country to high U.S. grocery prices.

“So while Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics,” El-Sayed said in a statement posted to the social platform X.

Support for Israel was a focal point of the widely watched Senate primary, with Stevens backed by millions from pro-Israel lobbying groups.

Since the primary, Stevens has supported El-Sayed and endorsed him immediately after. But Stevens’s fiancé, who is Jewish, recently said he would vote for former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers over El-Sayed.

Stevens reaffirmed that she would support El-Sayed in a CNN interview on Wednesday but said some Michigan voters are “hurt” and “confused” about the ad linking Israel to grocery prices.

She said in a statement on Friday that El-Sayed did not denounce the ad forcefully enough and expected him to apologize.

“The ad did not invent its argument; it dramatized one Dr. El-Sayed has made in his own words throughout this campaign: that Israel is the reason Michigan cannot afford schools, healthcare, and child care,” Stevens said. “I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well.”

Rogers has courted disaffected Democrats, mainly Jewish voters, as part of his effort to win Michigan in a Democratic-leaning year.

Stevens said she accepted an invitation from Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-S.C.), a major leader in the Black and Christian communities, to appear alongside the congressman and El-Sayed in a Detroit church service on Sunday.

The Hill reached out to both Stevens and El-Sayed to see if the joint appearance will continue as planned.

articles.title: New autism study complicates Trump administration’s search for cause
articles.body:
by Joseph Choi 10/31/26 06:00 AM ET

A recently published found associations between certain maternal health conditions during pregnancy and autism diagnoses across racial and ethnic groups, underscoring how much remains unknown as the Trump administration searches for a cause of autism.

Researchers from the New York University Grossman School of Medicine and the Kaiser Permanente School of Medicine published a study earlier this month that included 224 ,353 children born at Kaiser Permanente Northern California hospitals between 2010 and 2017.

Out of the more than 200,000 children, 2.4 percent were diagnosed with autism — not too far off from the 3.2 percentage rate reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Across different racial and ethnic groups, autism rates generally hovered around 2 and 3 percent.

But other findings stood out: Four out of 25 maternal health conditions — obesity, depressive episode, asthma and other maternal diseases complicating pregnancy — had a higher association with autism diagnoses when it came to white mothers than mothers who were Black, Hispanic or Asian and Pacific Islander.

Magdalena Janecka, associate professor at the Grossman School of Medicine’s department of child and adolescent psychiatry and co-author of the study, said the research highlighted the need to further examine environmental factors.

“I think this study highlights that the link between certain environmental factors and autism (and other conditions) is likely to be heterogeneous across different population groups: not because the fundamental biology differs, but because what these environmental factors entail may differ among different individuals,” Janecka said in written responses to The Hill.

She emphasized that these findings are “definitely not” indicative that “these maternal conditions cause autism.”

“Instead, it may indicate that some factors related to this maternal condition (e.g., genetic factors) are also implicated in autism. We still need to do more research to understand what exactly drives these effects,” she added.

That conclusion is unlikely to satisfy the Trump administration, as some have set out on a mission to find the cause of autism.

Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in April 2025 said the administration would determine the cause of rising autism rates by September of that year. When the deadline came around, he and President Trump speculated from the Oval Office that the common over-the-counter pain reliever acetaminophen taken during pregnancy could be linked to autism, without presenting new evidence.

This claim was denounced by maternal medicine groups and autism advocates alike. A month later, Kennedy walked back this claim somewhat, saying there “is not sufficient to say it definitely caused autism, but it is very suggestive.”

Kennedy has also long refused to discount the theory that vaccinations could be linked to autism, despite no evidence being found linking immunizations to later diagnoses. A CDC page published earlier this year claims “studies supporting a link have been ignored by health authorities.”

The overarching position of groups like the nonprofit Autism Speaks is that autism spectrum disorder develops as a result of both genetic and environmental influences. This is a position that Janecka shares.

“Our study neither supports nor challenges this,” said Janecka. “We don’t know what exactly drove the observations we reported, and so it is difficult to attribute them to either genetic or non-genetic factors.”

In discussing their findings, researchers acknowledged that differences in access to care, insurance continuity, clinical follow-up and treatment patterns could have affected what they observed.

An opinion piece published last year, co-authored by Janecka, argued differences in potential causes of childhood neuropsychiatric outcomes are “often overlooked,” with social determinants often filtered out of analyses.

“As race/ethnicity is primarily a social construct—associated with experiences of structural inequities, racism, and environmental injustice—that aligns poorly with genetic ancestry, we emphasize that the differences in the exposure–outcome associations across race/ethnic strata would arise largely because of societal, rather than biological, causes,” the authors wrote.

The study published this month took into account the history of underdiagnosis among certain groups, like the children of Black mothers being less likely to receive a diagnosis even when scoring high for autism-related traits in testing.

According to experts, autism does not occur at different rates across different races and ethnicities.

“We don’t have any evidence that shows that there’s any difference across race ethnicity in terms of autism diagnosis,” said Andy Shih, chief science officer of Autism Speaks.

“We do see … racial, ethnic differences in terms of diagnosis between white kids and Asian kids and African American kids, Hispanic kids for example,” Shih added. “But you know those gaps have been closing. So, I think the latest report that we have — it actually shows that at least at national level that we have closed the gap in terms of some ethnicity-based assessment.”

Shih hopes that the findings from the study bring more attention to the need for “the best healthcare access for expectant mothers.”

Janecka added, “What I would hope our study highlights is the need for more studies like ours stratifying the observed effects by maternal race/ethnicity, as well as considering other ways to stratify the total population: based on e.g., insurance status. I think rather than regress some differences out of our models, we should strive to better understand them.”

The Hill has reached out to HHS for comment.

articles.title: Judge blocks DOJ from threatening election officials over noncitizen voting claims
articles.body:
by Sarah Davis 10/30/26 11:01 PM ET

A California federal judge Friday ordered the Trump administration to stop threatening election officials with criminal prosecution in its ongoing efforts to crack down on noncitizen voting.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued a temporary restraining order connected to a lawsuit brought by unions representing California election workers earlier Friday. In her decision, the Biden-appointed judge noted Election Day was “around the corner.”

“Ballots have already been issued. Americans have already begun voting. Workers have already begun processing ballots,” Thompson wrote. “Given the consequences of inaction, the Court sees no reason to delay its ruling.”

The order also directs the Trump administration to halt its efforts to force these workers to remove certain people from voter rolls, deny ballot requests to some voters or set aside ballots for individuals it suspects are ineligible to vote.

The plaintiffs involved in this case include The Service Employees International Union; American Federation Of State, County and Municipal Employees; the League Of United Latin American Citizens and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People.

The initial complaint accuses Attorney General Todd Blanche and other top Justice Department (DOJ) officials of carrying out “a coordinated campaign to intimidate, threaten, and coerce state and local officials and employees.”

This week, the DOJ sent letters to election officials in all 50 states threatening potential prosecution if they failed to preserve election records.

The DOJ had sent similar correspondence a week prior to election officials in every California county, demanding they work with the federal government to identify potential noncitizens on their voter rolls. The letter warned these officials would “risk significant federal scrutiny” if they failed to comply with this request.

Earlier this week, another federal judge in California threw out the Trump administration’s lawsuit attempting to require the state to set aside the ballots of 20,000 people the federal government had identified as potential noncitizens. A split federal appeals court panel upheld this ruling Friday.

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ and the White House for comment on Thompson’s order.

articles.title: Democrats weigh Israel election results amid lingering uncertainty
articles.body:
by Mike Lillis 10/30/26 07:03 PM ET

The results of Israel’s elections this week have left Democrats on Capitol Hill with a mixed bag of emotions.

The lawmakers say they’re heartened by the massive voter turnout, the erosion of support for conservative Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and the potential influence of his top opponent, retired Gen. Gadi Eisenkot, over whatever governing coalition is ultimately formed.

Eisenkot is seen as a more moderate figure when it comes to Israeli-Palestinian relations, including his vows to rein in Israeli settler violence in the West Bank — a position that aligns him with Democrats in the Capitol.

“I hope it bodes well for a coalition, a governing coalition, who reject some of what I find are the most grievous errors of Netanyahu’s time,” Rep. Madeleine Dean (D-Pa.), a senior member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Friday by phone.

But the Democrats are also anxious about the lingering uncertainty surrounding the results, after all parties fell short of the 61 seats needed to lead the Knesset. And they’re voicing concerns about the stark national divisions reflected by the election, which was broadly viewed as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023, massacre against Israelis by Hamas terrorists.

“One of the signs is that there’s anything but unity in Israel, and so where do they go from here?” Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.), one of Israel’s most vocal congressional allies, said Friday, also in a phone interview. “Only time will tell.”

Schneider characterized Eisenkot as a more reasonable partner, citing his commitment to curbing West Bank violence by Israeli settlers.

“What they are doing is a threat to peace, and I think Eisenkot is more committed to thwarting that, and squashing it,” Schneider said. “That’s a critical thing.”

Still, Eisenkot is no liberal. And progressive Democrats are worried that, despite Eisenkot’s break from Netanyahu on issues like settler violence and the need for a deeper investigation into the Oct. 7 attack, both candidates oppose the creation of a Palestinian state — a development many Democrats consider to be a crucial part of any lasting peace deal in the region.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has repeatedly advocated for an autonomous Palestinian state as the only path to a long-term peace accord. His influence over the debate in Washington, D.C., is expected to grow tremendously, since Democrats are favored to control the House next year and Jeffries is in line to take the Speaker’s gavel.

Already, he’s promising to stage a vote on legislation to apply economic sanctions on anyone who engages in violence in the occupied West Bank, while barring them from entering the U.S. The bill has been sponsored by 175 House Democrats.

Dean is one of them. And she said the party should “absolutely” pass the bill if Democrats control the House next year.

“America needs to lead. We need to have our voices heard, and we can’t count on” Israeli leaders, she said. “We have to have some moral courage and authority to say, ‘No more.’

“This is a series of wrongs, including killing, that we must absolutely, loudly, condemn.”

Tuesday’s election in Israel was the first since the attack of Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas militants operating out of Gaza killed roughly 1,200 people and kidnapped 250 more.

The final results, unveiled Friday, left Netanyahu’s coalition with 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot’s bloc held 48 seats and a group of Arab parties won 19.

Democrats were quick to cheer the erosion of Netanyahu’s support, which fell from almost 70 seats before the elections.

“That was the Israeli people saying, ‘We want something different,’” Schneider said. “No one in Israel wants to sacrifice their security — that’s true whether they’re Jewish or Muslim. They all want their kids to grow up in safety and security.”

“But I think they want a change in direction from this government, which is unquestionably the most extreme government in Israel’s history,” he added. “And you saw in the election a drift away from that.”

What happens next remains unclear. The leaders of the various blocs are expected to huddle behind closed doors in an effort to forge some form of coalition that hits the 61-seat mark constituting a Knesset majority. The most likely scenarios include the formation of a unity government between the Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs.

Alternatively, Eisenkot’s group could join forces with the Arab parties, bonded by a shared opposition to Netanyahu.

If no such coalition can be built, Israel would stage another election.

In Washington, the Democrats’ approach to Israeli relations is likely to be influenced by the composition of the governing coalition and how it addresses things like settler violence.

“The actions the next government takes to address the extremist violence will most certainly affect how we look at either supporting the actions they’re taking, or putting pressure on [them] to take further action,” Schneider said.

Dean, for her part, said she’s encouraged by the rising influence of the Arab parties, whose 19 seats in the Knesset is a new high mark.

“What I do hope is, in these weeks and months coming up, more of the Arab voices and seats are heard and will change, will temper, whoever emerges as the leader,” she said.

The debate in Washington is also likely to be influenced by the incoming group of liberal lawmakers affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America. Those lawmakers have been highly critical of Israel’s human rights record toward Palestinians, and they’re expected to bring their activism to Capitol Hill.

Dean said there’s been a broader attitudinal shift toward Israel in Congress since Netanyahu began attacking Gaza, which has led to the death of more than 70,000 people. She’s excited at the prospect of having more Netanyahu critics in the Capitol.

“People were slow to separate Mr. Netanyahu from our love and support for Israel,” Dean said. “But I think we are well on our way, and I hope new members come in and help us make that argument in an even more robust way.”
